sources.title: Cape hare
sources.note: Cites Johnston, Robinson, Child and Relton (2019), IUCN Least Concern.

size.note: The 2025 EWT assessment gives size at maturity as 51 cm in males and 55 cm in females, and a maximum of 59 cm, without saying whether this is head-and-body length or total length. Animal Diversity Web gives a range length of 520–595 mm, which sits inside that span, and ear length of 12–14 cm. Animal Diversity Web also gives an unsexed mass of 4–5 kg, but that account mixes characters with the European brown hare, so mass is omitted rather than used. Shoulder height and a separate tail length were not found. Females are larger than males. Skinner and Chimimba (2005, p. 67) give, in Table 33.1 (all samples combined): tail 6.7–14.5 cm; mass 1.2–3 kg.

summary: A long-eared hare of open, dry grassland. The coat is a fine light brown, reddish or sandy grey, and a white ring usually surrounds the eye. Females are larger than males. It is mainly nocturnal and usually solitary. It is on the 2011 SANParks Kruger checklist. Resident status follows one research-grade record at Skukuza on 4 March 2025, whose community taxon is Lepus capensis. The 2025 regional range does not include the Lowveld and was not used for status.
description: A typical hare, with long hind legs built for leaping and running, large eyes, and long ears. A white ring usually surrounds the eye. The fine, soft coat varies from light brown to reddish to sandy grey. Animal Diversity Web describes ginger-brown upperparts with some black shading, a paler ginger wash on the breast and sides, white inner legs and belly, a reddish-grey nape, and black-tipped ears 12–14 cm long, but that account appears to mix characters with the European brown hare and is used with caution. Females are larger than males. In the field it is easily confused with the scrub hare (Lepus saxatilis); a published distinction is in the upper incisors, which is not a field character.
habits: Predominantly nocturnal, and only occasionally seen by day in overcast weather. Usually solitary, except when a female is in oestrus. In the Free State, home ranges of about 6.5 ha for males and 8.3 ha for females have been recorded; ranges may overlap at the edges and vary with habitat. It can live without standing water, taking moisture from its food.

diet.summary: A herbivore that both grazes and browses. It often prefers short green grasses, but diet shifts with habitat: an East African study found mostly Digitaria and Eragrostis grasses, whereas Cape hares in the Karoo were recorded browsing shrubs such as Galenia fruticosa and Osteospermum sinuatum and were not seen eating grass. Like other hares, it may recycle droppings to extract more nutrients.
items: shrub foliage, including in the Karoo Galenia fruticosa and Osteospermum sinuatum

young: Breeding can take place all year, but in southern Africa most births have been recorded between July and December. Gestation is about 42 days (Animal Diversity Web gives 38–41 days). Litters are usually of one to three leverets, with up to four litters a year in one Free State study, and as many as eight litters suggested in a wider review; Animal Diversity Web gives a wider litter range of one to six. The young are precocial: they are born with their eyes open and can move about shortly after birth. A Kruger-specific birth season was not found.

predators.note: Vulpes chama. Named as a predator in a Free State diet study cited by the 2025 regional assessment; the species is not in this Kruger guide.
Polemaetus bellicosus. In one Cape study cited by the 2025 regional assessment, hares made up half of the diet.
Aquila verreauxii. Named as a predator in the 2025 regional assessment.

habitat: A wide range of dry, open grassland and other open habitats, including Nama-Karoo and Succulent Karoo, and parts of the Grassland and Savannah biomes. It avoids only bushy or closed cover, and will move onto burnt ground once the grass begins to sprout. A Kruger-specific habitat account was not found, and the 2025 regional range description does not name the Lowveld.

similar.note: Field identification of Cape and scrub hares is often uncertain, and the two are easily confused. A published distinction is in the shape of the upper incisors, which is not a field character. The Cape hare prefers dry, open country and avoids bushy or closed cover, whereas the scrub hare is associated with grass cover in savannah woodland and scrub, but the ranges overlap.

population.notes: No Kruger population figure was found. Regional densities (4.7–24.8 hares/km² in South Africa, and 16.5 individuals/km² on Benfontein Game Farm in the Northern Cape) are not Kruger counts. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf. The 2025 regional assessment lists a declining trend for the assessment region, not for Kruger.

ears.shape: long, and described as black-tipped and 12–14 cm in one compiled account

upperparts.pattern: fine, soft coat; colour varies across this range

underparts.pattern: inner sides of the legs and the belly described as white in one compiled account

legs.colour: white on the inner sides in one compiled account

viewNotes.note: Long ears, a usually white eye-ring, and a fine coat that runs from light brown to reddish or sandy grey.

calls.description: Mostly silent. A high-pitched scream is given when the hare is handled or caught in a trap, and a barely audible grunt has also been noted.

research.note: The English and Afrikaans names follow the 2011 SANParks checklist (Cape hare, Vlakhaas); the 2025 EWT page also gives Vlakhaas. The 2025 EWT range does not include Kruger or the Lowveld, so rule (b) does not apply, and the 2011 checklist was not used on its own. Status is resident with months 1–12 under rule (c): iNaturalist observation 264080608, observed on 4 March 2025 at Skukuza, is research-grade and not captive, and the community taxon is Lepus capensis. An earlier identification of that observation as the scrub hare was replaced and is not the current community identification. The photograph has no reusable licence and is not used as an image. No Kruger population figure was found. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf. Animal Diversity Web appears to mix characters with the European brown hare, so its mass figure and some habit details were not used.

gaps: No Kruger population figure was found. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf

No reusable Kruger photograph was found (0 licensed research-grade photographs in iNaturalist place 69020). The five photographs are research-grade records from South Africa outside Kruger. A rear-view thumbnail (observation 171254640) was not used.
iNaturalist has 0 sound observations for Lepus capensis in place 69020. No sourced vocalisation description was found, so calls is empty.

Shoulder height and a mass figure that can be used with confidence for this species were not found. Animal Diversity Web gives 4–5 kg, but that account appears to mix characters with the European brown hare, so mass is omitted.
The 2025 EWT length figures (51–59 cm) do not say whether they are head-and-body or total length.
A Kruger-specific habitat account and a Kruger-specific birth-month range were not found. Southern African accounts give most births between July and December.
Field marks that reliably separate Cape and scrub hares in a photograph, other than the upper incisors (Robinson 1986, cited in the 2016 assessment), were not found in the sources used.

Iris colour, ear colour as a named value, face, muzzle and tail colour were not given clearly in the sources used, so those marks are null. Stuart's field guide was not available. Skinner and Chimimba (2005) was used for the fields named in its source entry.
